detail.packageQuoteTitle: How to read your package quote without surprises
detail.packageQuoteIntro: Hospital packages in India are quoted as all-inclusive bundles, but the exact scope varies. Always confirm these items before committing:
detail.packageQuoteItem1Desc: Usually included, but verify if senior consultant fees are extra.
detail.packageQuoteItem2Desc: Stents, valves, mesh, or joint implants may be billed separately. Ask for the brand and price range.
detail.packageQuoteItem3Desc: Standard packages include a shared or private ward for a fixed number of days. Extra days or ICU upgrades are charged additionally.
detail.packageQuoteItem4Desc: Pre-operative tests are typically included, but advanced imaging (PET, cardiac MRI) may not be.
detail.packageQuoteItem5Desc: For transplant and blood-disorder treatments, donor workup, donor charges, and blood products are often billed separately.
detail.packageQuoteItem6Desc: Take-home medications are usually not included. Budget an additional $50 to $200 depending on the procedure.
detail.decisionFrameworkIntro: Before choosing a hospital or committing to travel, use this checklist to compare options objectively:
detail.decisionFrameworkItem1: Is the hospital JCI, NABH, or ISO accredited?
detail.decisionFrameworkItem2: Does the surgeon perform this procedure at least 50 times per year?
detail.decisionFrameworkItem3: Is the quoted price all-inclusive, or are implants, ICU, and tests extra?
detail.decisionFrameworkItem4: What is the hospital's success rate and infection rate for this specific procedure?
detail.decisionFrameworkItem5: Will you receive your full medical records, imaging, and a discharge summary in English before flying home?
detail.decisionFrameworkItem6: Is there a dedicated international-patient team for visa, airport pickup, accommodation, and language support?
detail.decisionFrameworkItem7: What happens if there is a complication after you return home? Is telemedicine follow-up included?
detail.decisionFrameworkItem8: Does the hospital accept your insurance, or can they provide documents for your TPA to process reimbursement?

faqs.question: What is Honest Second Opinion?
faqs.answer: Honest Second Opinion is a doctor-led review of your diagnosis, scans, reports, and proposed treatment plan designed to help you understand whether surgery is truly needed, what alternatives exist, and what the safest next step could be.

faqs.question: Why should I take a second opinion?
Which conditions can I get reviewed?
faqs.answer: You can reach out to us for conditions spanning:
bullets: Orthopaedic issues (knee, shoulder, spine, joint pain)
General surgery conditions such as hernia, piles, gallstones
Vascular conditions such as varicose veins

faqs.question: What reports should I upload?
faqs.answer: Please upload all necessary information to help us understand your concern completely. This can include:
faqs.answerSuffix: You can upload multiple files together.

faqs.question: Can surgery really be avoided?
faqs.answer: In many cases, yes. Some conditions improve with medication, physiotherapy, lifestyle changes, monitoring, or minimally invasive treatment. If surgery is necessary, we'll tell you honestly.

faqs.question: Is the second opinion really free?
faqs.answer: Yes. Reviewing your reports and sharing an honest opinion is completely free, with no obligation to book treatment or travel with us.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get my second opinion?
faqs.answer: In most cases you will receive a specialist's response within 24 hours of sharing complete reports. Complex cases may take up to 48 hours.

faqs.question: What if I don't have all my reports?
faqs.answer: Send what you have. Our care team will tell you exactly which test or report the specialist needs before giving a reliable opinion.

faqs.question: Who reviews my reports?
faqs.answer: Your case is reviewed by a senior, board-certified specialist in the relevant field at one of our accredited partner hospitals in India.

faqs.question: Will you share my medical data with anyone else?
faqs.answer: No. Your reports are shared only with the reviewing specialist and the hospital you approve. We follow strict data protection practices.

faqs.question: What happens after I receive the opinion?
faqs.answer: The choice is yours. If treatment is recommended and you wish to proceed, we provide a full cost estimate, visa assistance, and travel planning. If not, you simply have peace of mind — free of charge.

faqs.question: Is a second opinion the same as a teleconsultation?
faqs.answer: No. A second opinion is a written review of your existing reports and diagnosis by a specialist who has not met you. A teleconsultation is a live video appointment where the doctor examines you in real time. A second opinion is faster, cheaper, and does not require travel — but it cannot replace a physical examination. If the reviewing specialist recommends an in-person assessment, we will tell you.

faqs.question: Can a second opinion change my diagnosis?
faqs.answer: Yes. In a Mayo Clinic study of 286 referred patients, 21% received a completely different diagnosis and 66% received a refined or redefined diagnosis. Only 12% had their original diagnosis confirmed. A second opinion can confirm, refine, or change your diagnosis — and this can change your entire treatment plan.

faqs.question: What if the second opinion differs from my first doctor's recommendation?
faqs.answer: This is common and not a sign that either doctor is wrong. Medicine often has more than one reasonable approach. If the opinions differ, we recommend sharing the second opinion with your first doctor and asking them to explain the difference. If you are still unsure, a third opinion or a multidisciplinary tumor board review (for cancer cases) can help. We can arrange either.

faqs.question: Does insurance cover a second opinion?
faqs.answer: Many international insurance plans cover second opinions, especially for major surgery or cancer treatment. Check with your insurer whether 'remote second opinion' or 'international specialist review' is covered. We can provide an invoice or letter of medical necessity if your insurer requires documentation. However, our second opinion is free regardless of insurance — you do not need coverage to use it.

faqs.question: How is this different from asking another doctor in my own country?
faqs.answer: A second opinion from India gives you access to specialists at JCI- and NABH-accredited hospitals who see high volumes of complex cases at a fraction of Western costs. If you are already considering treatment in India, the second opinion also tells you whether travel is worthwhile before you book flights. A local second opinion cannot tell you what treatment in India would cost or involve.

secondOpinion.definitionTitle: What is a second medical opinion?
secondOpinion.definitionBody: A second medical opinion is an independent review of your diagnosis, test results, and proposed treatment plan by a qualified specialist who has not been involved in your care. It is not a sign of distrust in your first doctor — it is a normal, expected part of informed decision-making, especially before surgery, cancer treatment, or any major procedure. A second opinion can confirm your diagnosis, refine it, change it, or suggest alternative treatments you may not have been offered.
secondOpinion.statsTitle: Why a second opinion matters — the evidence
secondOpinion.statsIntro: Research from leading institutions shows that second opinions frequently change the diagnosis or treatment plan. These are not marketing claims — they are published findings.

secondOpinion.statsCaveat: These figures come from a single academic medical center in the United States and may not reflect every healthcare system. They illustrate why a second opinion is worth seeking — not that your first doctor is wrong.
secondOpinion.whenNotTitle: When a second opinion is NOT enough
secondOpinion.whenNotBody: A remote second opinion cannot replace a physical examination, emergency care, or hands-on assessment. Do not wait for a second opinion if:
whenNotItems: You are in a life-threatening emergency — call your local emergency number immediately
Your doctor has advised urgent treatment and delaying could cause harm
You have acute symptoms (chest pain, difficulty breathing, sudden weakness, severe bleeding)
You are already in active treatment and experiencing a crisis
secondOpinion.whenNotNote: A second opinion is a planning tool, not an emergency service. If someone is in immediate danger, call local emergency services first, then contact us for India treatment planning.

secondOpinion.languagesNote: Hospital interpreters are also available for Arabic, French, and Russian at partner hospitals.
secondOpinion.conditionsTitle: When a second opinion matters most
secondOpinion.conditionsIntro: Some situations carry higher stakes and benefit more from an independent review. If any of these apply to you, a second opinion is strongly recommended.

conditions.when: New diagnosis, proposed change in treatment, or rare/advanced cancer
conditions.why: Treatment paths vary widely; a multidisciplinary review can confirm staging and suggest alternatives

conditions.when: Advised bypass, valve surgery, or complex intervention
conditions.why: Cardiology often has medical vs surgical options; a second review can clarify which is right for you

conditions.when: Brain or spine surgery is recommended
conditions.why: Neurosurgical decisions are often irreversible; confirming the plan and approach is critical

conditions.when: Joint replacement, spine surgery, or sports injury surgery
conditions.why: Many orthopaedic conditions improve with physiotherapy or minimally invasive options first
Transplant timing, donor matching, and center choice affect outcomes significantly

conditions.when: IVF has failed or a different protocol is suggested
conditions.why: Protocols vary between clinics; a second review can identify alternative approaches

secondOpinion.questionsTitle: Questions to ask during your second opinion
secondOpinion.questionsIntro: A second opinion is most useful when you ask focused questions. Print or save these and share them with your reviewing specialist.
questions: Do you agree with my diagnosis, or would you order additional tests to confirm it?
Is the recommended treatment the only option, or are there alternatives?
What are the risks and benefits of each treatment option?
What happens if I delay treatment or choose no treatment?
Are there less invasive options that could work for my case?
What is the expected recovery time and outcome for each option?
How many of these procedures has the recommended hospital performed?
What will the total cost be, including pre-op, surgery, and recovery?
Are there clinical trials or newer treatments I should consider?
What follow-up care will I need after returning home?
secondOpinion.differsTitle: What if the second opinion differs from my first doctor's recommendation?
secondOpinion.differsBody: This is common and does not mean either doctor is wrong. Medicine often has more than one reasonable approach. If the opinions differ, we recommend: (1) sharing the second opinion with your first doctor and asking them to explain the difference; (2) asking both doctors what evidence supports their recommendation; (3) if still unsure, requesting a third opinion or a multidisciplinary tumor board review for cancer cases. We can arrange any of these. The goal is not to find the 'right' doctor — it is to make the most informed decision for your specific case.
secondOpinion.limitationsBody: A remote second opinion is based on the reports and imaging you provide. It cannot replace a physical examination, hands-on assessment, or direct observation of your condition. If the reviewing specialist recommends an in-person consultation before a final decision, we will tell you honestly. A second opinion is a planning tool to help you decide whether to proceed, delay, or seek alternatives — it is not a guarantee of outcome.
